:::{#def-lu}
#### LU factorization

An **LU factorization** of an $n \times n$ matrix $\matr{A}$ is a product
$\matr{A} = \matr{L} \matr{U}$
with $\matr{L}$ unit lower triangular and $\matr{U}$ upper triangular (@def-triangular-matrix).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-lu}
#### An LU factorization of a $3 \times 3$ matrix

Let
$\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ -3 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$,
$\matr{L} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{3}{2} & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
(unit lower triangular) and
$\matr{U} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$
(upper triangular).
By @def-matrix-mult, entry $(i, j)$ of $\matr{L} \matr{U}$ is $\sum_k \ell_{ik}\,u_{kj}$,
so row $i$ of $\matr{L} \matr{U}$ is $\sum_k \ell_{ik}$ times row $k$ of $\matr{U}$.
Row 1 is $1 \cd (2, 1, -1) = (2, 1, -1)$;
row 2 is $-\tfrac{3}{2}\,(2, 1, -1) + (0, \tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}) = (-3, -1, 2)$,
and row 3 is $-(2, 1, -1) + 4\,(0, \tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}) + (0, 0, -1) = (-2, 1, 2)$.
These are the rows of $\matr{A}$, so $\matr{L} \matr{U} = \matr{A}$ is an LU factorization.
The below-diagonal entries of $\matr{L}$ are the negatives of the multiples of earlier rows
that Gaussian elimination adds to reduce $\matr{A}$ to $\matr{U}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-not-lu}
#### An invertible matrix with no LU factorization

$\matr{P} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ is invertible:
$\matr{P}^2 = \matr{I}_2$, so $\matr{P}^{-1} = \matr{P}$ (@def-matrix-inverse);
but it has no LU factorization.
If $\matr{P} = \matr{L} \matr{U}$, the $(1, 1)$ entry gives $0 = 1 \cd u_{11}$, so $u_{11} = 0$,
and then the $(2, 1)$ entry gives $1 = \ell_{21}\,u_{11} = 0$, which is impossible.
Swapping the two rows first removes the obstacle:
the swapped matrix is $\matr{I}_2 = \matr{I}_2\,\matr{I}_2$.

:::
